notes.b: Science is not done by one person or one country working alone. Scientists everywhere work on shared problems and build on each other’s published results, and that is what makes it a global enterprise.
points: Scientists in many countries work on the same problems, share data and build on each other’s published results. Knowledge is not owned by one country or person.
Because claims are tested by people with different backgrounds and assumptions, mistakes and hidden bias are more likely to be spotted than if one group checked its own work.

Large problems need international teams, shared funding and shared equipment. The Human Genome Project (1990–2003) sequenced the human genome (read out all of a person’s DNA) through an international consortium of 20 research groups in six countries: the USA, the UK, Japan, France, Germany and China.
Under the Bermuda Principles (1996), the Human Genome Project released its sequence data publicly within 24 hours, free for anyone to use, so other researchers could start work straight away.

Speed through sharing: in January 2020 Chinese scientists published the genome sequence of the new coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) online. Research groups around the world used it within days to design tests and begin developing vaccines.

Funding is international too. Irish researchers are funded by Research Ireland, the state agency formed in 2024 from Science Foundation Ireland and the Irish Research Council, and by the EU research programme Horizon Europe (2021–2027), which funds teams that include several countries.

Science needs four things to work across borders: clear communication, international conventions, peer review and reproducibility. Each gets its own block below. There is more on funding as a source of bias in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.
notes.tip: If asked why science is a global enterprise, give the idea (shared data, shared funding, claims tested by different people) and back it with a named example such as the Human Genome Project or the SARS-CoV-2 genome shared in January 2020.

notes.b: A discovery only helps science once other scientists can read it, understand it and use it. So scientists publish in a standard form and use precise language that anyone in the field can follow.
points: Scientists communicate mainly through papers in scientific journals. They also use conferences, review articles (summaries of many studies on one topic) and shared online databases such as genome databases (stores of DNA sequences).

A research paper has a standard structure: title and authors; abstract (a short summary); introduction (background and the aim or hypothesis); methods (exactly what was done, with materials and conditions).
The paper then gives results (data in tables and graphs); discussion (what the results mean, the limitations, and comparison with other work); and references to other work.
The methods section must be detailed enough for another scientist to repeat the work, which makes reproducibility (others getting the same result) possible.

Scientific language must be precise and unambiguous. Terms have one agreed meaning (e.g. “theory” in science is not “a guess”), quantities are given with units, and uncertainty is stated rather than hidden. English is the main shared language of international science.
Open access journals make papers free to read for everyone, not only subscribers, so more people can use the findings.

Preprints are papers posted online before peer review (checking by independent experts), e.g. on bioRxiv, launched 2013, and medRxiv, launched 2019, for medical research. They speed up sharing, as in the COVID-19 pandemic, but readers must remember that they have not yet been checked.

Poor communication slows science. Gregor Mendel published his results on inheritance in pea plants in 1866, in the journal of the Natural History Society of Brünn (now Brno, Czech Republic). They were little read, and their importance was recognised only when other scientists reached the same conclusions independently in 1900.
Communicating with the public (news, policy and outreach) is also part of a scientist’s work. There is more on this in Evaluating evidence.
notes.tip: Mendel is the standard example of poor communication delaying science: his 1866 results were little read until 1900. When you mention preprints, say they are not yet peer reviewed.

notes.b: For scientists in different countries to compare and repeat each other’s work, they must use the same units, names and rules. These shared agreements are called international conventions.
points: An international convention is a set of rules or standards agreed by scientists or governments across countries, so that results mean the same everywhere and can be compared and repeated. Standards also cover laboratory safety signs (hazard symbols) and depositing data in public databases.

SI units (Système International) are the agreed units of measurement: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), mole (amount of substance) and kelvin (temperature), with degrees Celsius also widely used.
Prefixes such as milli- and micro- are used with SI units, e.g. mm, and µm, the unit for cell sizes. The unit nm is used for organelles and molecules, which are smaller still.

Binomial nomenclature gives each species a two-part Latin name, genus then species, e.g. Homo sapiens. The genus starts with a capital letter, the species name is lower case, and the name is printed in italics or underlined when handwritten.

Carl Linnaeus established the system; the starting point for plant names is his Species Plantarum (1753). One scientific name avoids confusion between common names, which differ between languages and regions. There is more on this in Classification.

Other naming conventions: human genes have agreed symbols, written in italics, e.g. the CFTR gene, whose faulty alleles (versions of a gene) cause cystic fibrosis. The protein is written without italics. Chemical names and formulas follow agreed rules, e.g. CO₂ and C₆H₁₂O₆.

Ethical conventions set rules for research. The Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 1964) sets out ethical principles for research on people, including informed consent and independent ethical review. It followed the Nuremberg Code (1947), which was written after the trials of Nazi doctors.

The Convention on Biological Diversity (1992, agreed at the Rio Earth Summit) commits countries to conserving biodiversity, using it sustainably and sharing fairly the benefits of genetic resources. CITES (1973) controls international trade in endangered species.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain why conventions such as SI units and binomial names are needed. The answer is that results and species names then mean the same in every country, so they can be compared and repeated.

notes.b: Before a paper is published, other experts check it. This is peer review, the main quality check in science, and it follows a set sequence of steps.
points: Peer review is the evaluation of a scientific paper by independent experts in the same field, the author’s “peers”, before it is published.

Steps 1 to 3: the scientists submit the paper to a journal; the editor checks that it suits the journal and is of reasonable quality, and may reject it straight away; if it passes, the editor sends it to usually two or three independent experts, called reviewers or referees.

Step 4: the reviewers check whether the methods are suitable, the data support the conclusions, the analysis is sound, the work is original and important, ethical rules were followed and other work is properly referenced.
Step 5: they recommend accept, accept with minor revisions, revise and resubmit (major revisions), or reject.
Steps 6 and 7: the authors revise the paper and reply to each comment, and the editor makes the final decision before the paper is published.
Single-blind review: the reviewers know who the authors are, but the authors do not know the reviewers. This lets reviewers judge freely, but they may be swayed by the authors’ reputation.
Double-blind review: neither side knows the other, which reduces bias from the authors’ reputation, gender or country. Open review: names, and sometimes reports, are published.
Diagram: a flowchart of the seven steps, with a loop from “revise” back to “reviewers”.
notes.tip: If asked what peer review is and why it matters, define it (independent experts check a paper before publication) and give a purpose: it filters out poor work and improves papers. Learn the seven steps in order for the flowchart.

notes.h: Strengths and limits of peer review
notes.b: Peer review is valuable, but it is not a guarantee of truth. Knowing what it can and cannot do explains why scientists keep checking work after it is published.
points: Peer review filters out poor-quality or unsupported work, improves papers before publication, and gives readers some confidence in published work. A peer-reviewed paper is a more reliable source than one that is not. There is more on this in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.
Reviewers do not normally repeat the experiments, so they cannot detect well-hidden fraud or errors in raw data. Peer review does not guarantee that a paper is correct.
Reviewers can be biased, e.g. against ideas that challenge their own, or towards famous laboratories. The process is slow, and reviewers are usually unpaid volunteers.
Some low-quality “predatory” journals charge authors to publish while doing little or no real review, so a paper in such a journal has not really been checked.

Checking continues after publication. Other scientists read, cite and try to repeat the work; errors lead to published corrections, and serious errors or misconduct lead to retraction, when the journal withdraws the paper.

Hwang Woo-suk’s team published papers in the journal Science in 2004 and 2005 claiming to have made stem cells from cloned human embryos. The data were found to be fabricated, and the papers were retracted in 2006. Peer review had not caught the fraud; scrutiny after publication did.
notes.tip: Never write that peer review guarantees a paper is correct. Give strengths and limits as pairs, and use Hwang Woo-suk (fabricated data, retracted 2006) as the example of fraud that peer review missed.

notes.b: One result on its own is not enough to count as knowledge. Science accepts a finding only when others can get the same result, which is why reproducibility matters.
points: A result is reproducible if other scientists, working independently in other laboratories, get the same result when they repeat the work, using the same or different methods. There is more on repeatability and reproducibility in Objectivity and data quality.

Science relies on reproducibility because a single result may be due to chance, error, an unusual sample, bias or fraud. Agreement between independent groups shows that the result is a real feature of nature.

Only reproduced findings become accepted knowledge and can support theories. For example, the H. pylori explanation of stomach ulcers (that a bacterium causes them) was accepted once others reproduced the findings.
Reproducibility depends on clear communication: full methods, raw data and materials must be shared so that others can repeat the work.

Not all published results reproduce. Scientists at the company Amgen reported in 2012 that they could confirm the findings of only 6 of 53 “landmark” preclinical cancer studies (early studies done before testing in patients).
Causes of failure include small samples, selective reporting of positive results, pressure to publish, poorly described methods and, rarely, fraud.
Responses include sharing data openly, registering study plans in advance and publishing replication studies (repeats of earlier work), so that results are checked and not hidden if they disagree.
notes.tip: To explain why results must be reproduced before they are accepted, say a single result could be due to chance, error, bias or fraud, and that agreement between independent groups shows it is real.

keyTerms.definition: The evaluation of a scientific paper by independent experts in the same field before it is published.
An independent expert who reviews a submitted paper for a journal and recommends whether it is accepted, revised or rejected.
Peer review in which the reviewers know who the authors are but the authors do not know the reviewers.
Peer review in which neither the authors nor the reviewers know each other’s identity.
The withdrawal of a published paper by its journal, usually because of serious error or misconduct.
A paper posted online before peer review, so it has not yet been checked.
A journal whose papers are free for everyone to read, not only subscribers.
A set of rules or standards agreed across countries so that results can be compared and repeated.
The two-part Latin name of a species, genus followed by species, e.g. Homo sapiens.
The property of a result that other scientists, working independently, obtain again when they repeat the work.

questions.prompt: Describe the process of peer review and give one limitation of it.
questions.model: Peer review is the evaluation of a scientific paper by independent experts in the same field, the author’s peers, before it is published. First, the scientists submit the paper to a journal. Second, the editor checks that it suits the journal and is of reasonable quality, and may reject it straight away. Third, the editor sends it to usually two or three independent reviewers. Fourth, the reviewers check whether the methods are suitable, the data support the conclusions, the analysis is sound, the work is original and important, ethical rules were followed and other work is properly referenced. Fifth, they recommend accept, accept with minor revisions, revise and resubmit, or reject. Sixth, the authors revise the paper and reply to each comment. Seventh, the editor makes the final decision and the paper is published. One limitation is that reviewers do not normally repeat the experiments, so they cannot detect well-hidden fraud or errors in raw data. Peer review does not guarantee that a paper is correct.

questions.prompt: What is meant by reproducibility? Explain why scientists insist that results are reproducible.
questions.model: A result is reproducible if other scientists, working independently in other laboratories, get the same result when they repeat the work, using the same or different methods. Scientists insist on reproducibility because a single result may be due to chance, error, an unusual sample, bias or fraud. Agreement between independent groups shows that the result is a real feature of nature, and only reproduced findings become accepted knowledge that can support theories.

questions.prompt: Give two examples of international conventions used in biology and explain why each is needed.
questions.model: First, SI units are the agreed units of measurement, such as the metre, kilogram, second, mole and kelvin. They are needed so that measurements mean the same thing in every country and results can be compared and repeated. Second, binomial nomenclature gives each species a two-part Latin name, genus then species, e.g. Homo sapiens. It is needed because common names differ between languages and regions, and one scientific name avoids confusion.
